title: How am I using my soul?
hook: ask often: what am I using my soul for right now? (Meditations 5.11)
carry: what am I using it for

segments.voice: Yesterday: back to it. Your line was a sponge and egg. After a slip, did you skip the speech and take the next small step? Day five hundred sixty-eight.

Your phone has a battery screen that shows exactly where the power went. Maps, twelve percent. Messages, twenty. That one game, a slightly embarrassing forty. Nobody has a screen like that for attention, or for the inner life. If you did, what would today's breakdown say? Marcus Aurelius didn't have the screen, but he had the question, and he wrote it down as a short, sharp check. Today: how am I using my soul?
screen: `THE BATTERY SCREEN.` → `WHERE DID THE POWER GO?` → `HOW AM I USING MY SOUL?`

segments.voice: First, the question. What am I using my soul for right now? Marcus writes this in the eleventh entry of book five, and he says to ask it on every occasion. Not once a year at a retreat. Now, and now again. Second, the ruling part. Then he sharpens it. What is going on, he asks, in the part of me they call the ruling part? The Stoics' word was hegemonikon: the steering center of a person, where judgments and choices happen. Marcus wants to check who's at the wheel. Third, whose soul is it? And then the striking part. Whose soul do I have right now? A child's? A teenager's? A tyrant's? A farm animal's? A wild beast's? It's almost funny, and it's very honest. On some days a person might cycle through several of these: the child who wants it now, the tyrant who wants it done my way, the grazing animal scrolling for the next bite, the wild animal in traffic. Fourth, why ask often. The question isn't a test you pass. It's a mirror you keep glancing at. Each time you ask, you get a little gap: you notice the tyrant, and the noticing can loosen his grip. Asked often enough, it becomes a habit of returning, which was yesterday's whole lesson. Here's the plain version for an ordinary day. Three times, stop and ask: what am I using my soul for, right now? You don't have to fix the answer. Just hear it.
screen: `WHAT AM I USING MY SOUL FOR NOW?` · `THE RULING PART: WHO'S STEERING?` · `CHILD, TYRANT, OR WILD BEAST?` · `A MIRROR TO GLANCE AT OFTEN.` · then, large: `WHAT AM I USING IT FOR.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Ask it now: what am I using my soul for, right now? Listen for the honest answer. Maybe it's resting. Maybe it's half here and half in an email. Then ask Marcus's second question, lightly: whose soul is this, at the moment? A child's, impatient? A tyrant's, insisting? Something calmer? Don't judge it. Just name it. Then pick two more times today when you'll ask again. The bell holds the time.
Hegemonikon. Marcus's word for the ruling part, the steering center where judgments and choices happen. Today's word.
Your line: what am I using it for. Ask it three times today, morning, afternoon and evening, and just hear the answer. Day five hundred sixty-eight.

original.note: Greek, 'the ruling part': the Stoic name for the mind's steering center, from hegemon, 'leader'.

trapdoor: what it means: check, often, what your soul is being used for and who is steering it.
what a scholar hears: hegemonikon, from hegemon, 'leader', the Stoic seat of judgment and choice; our 'hegemony' comes from the same root.
recall: blood, bones, a net of nerves

notes: 5.11 paraphrased: about what am I now employing my soul? On every occasion ask this, and inquire, what have I now in this part of me which they call the ruling principle? and whose soul have I now? that of a child, a young man, a feeble woman, a tyrant, a domestic animal, a wild beast? The script gives child, teenager (young man), tyrant, farm animal, wild beast and omits 'a feeble woman'. Confirm the omission is acceptable.
hegemonikon and English 'hegemony' from hegemon: standard; confirm.
